The **Mississippi River**[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River#cite_note-24) is the [primary river](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_stem "Main stem") of the largest drainage basin in the United States.[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River#cite_note-25)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River#cite_note-26) It is the second-longest river in the U.S. after the [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_River "Missouri River").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River#cite_note-USGSlongest-27) From its traditional source of [Lake Itasca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Itasca "Lake Itasca") in northern [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota"), it flows generally south for 2,340 mi (3,766 km)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River#cite_note-USGSlongest-27) to the [Mississippi River Delta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River_Delta "Mississippi River Delta") in the [Gulf of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico"). With its many [tributaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tributaries "Tributaries"), the Mississippi's [watershed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage_basin "Drainage basin") drains all or parts of 32 [U.S. states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state "U.S.

state") and two [Canadian provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_provinces "Canadian provinces") between the [Rocky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mountains "Rocky Mountains") and [Appalachian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Mountains "Appalachian Mountains") mountains.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River#cite_note-28) The river either borders or passes through the states of Minnesota, [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin "Wisconsin"), [Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa "Iowa"), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"), [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri"), [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky "Kentucky"), [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee"), [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"), [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi"), and [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River#cite_note-29)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River#cite_note-30) The [main stem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_stem "Main stem") is entirely within the United States; the total [drainage basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage_basin "Drainage basin") is 1,151,000 mi 2 (2,980,000 km 2), of which only about one percent is in Canada. The Mississippi ranks as the world's [tenth-largest river](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_rivers_by_discharge "List of rivers by discharge") by discharge flow, and the largest in North America.

River lengths or river-length data are affected not only by some of the natural and artificial causes noted in the preceding paragraph, but also by the precision of various techniques of measurement, by the scale of available maps or aerial photographs, and by somewhat arbitrary decisions. For example, the length may be considered to be the distance from the mouth to the most distant headwater source (irrespective of stream name) or from the mouth to the headwaters of the stream commonly identified as the source stream. The names of some rivers, such as the Mississippi River and the Rio Grande, are unchanged from source to mouth. In contrast, the name of the source of the Mobile River—Tickanetley Creek—changes five times before becoming Mobile River 45 miles north of Mobile Bay. The lengths of meandering rivers, such as the Mississippi River south of Cairo, Ill., undergo significant changes in length from time to time because of a natural or excavated cutoff (a channel severing a narrow strip of land, thus bypassing a large bend in a river) that reduces river length and therefore navigation time. For example, between 1766 and 1885, the length of the Mississippi River from Cairo, Ill., to New Orleans, La., was reduced by 218 miles because of 18 cutoffs (Elliott, 1932, page 59).

texts.10: state") and two [Canadian provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_provinces "Canadian provinces") between the [Rocky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mountains "Rocky Mountains") and [Appalachian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Mountains "Appalachian Mountains") mountains.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River#cite_note-28) The river either borders or passes through the states of Minnesota, [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin "Wisconsin"), [Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa "Iowa"), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"), [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri"), [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky "Kentucky"), [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee"), [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"), [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi"), and [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River#cite_note-29)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River#cite_note-30) The [main stem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_stem "Main stem") is entirely within the United States; the total [drainage basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage_basin "Drainage basin") is 1,151,000 mi 2 (2,980,000 km 2), of which only about one percent is in Canada. The Mississippi ranks as the world's [tenth-largest river](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_rivers_by_discharge "List of rivers by discharge") by discharge flow, and the largest in North America.

River lengths or river-length data are affected not only by some of the natural and artificial causes noted in the preceding paragraph, but also by the precision of various techniques of measurement, by the scale of available maps or aerial photographs, and by somewhat arbitrary decisions. For example, the length may be considered to be the distance from the mouth to the most distant headwater source (irrespective of stream name) or from the mouth to the headwaters of the stream commonly identified as the source stream. The names of some rivers, such as the Mississippi River and the Rio Grande, are unchanged from source to mouth. In contrast, the name of the source of the Mobile River—Tickanetley Creek—changes five times before becoming Mobile River 45 miles north of Mobile Bay. The lengths of meandering rivers, such as the Mississippi River south of Cairo, Ill., undergo significant changes in length from time to time because of a natural or excavated cutoff (a channel severing a narrow strip of land, thus bypassing a large bend in a river) that reduces river length and therefore navigation time. For example, between 1766 and 1885, the length of the Mississippi River from Cairo, Ill., to New Orleans, La., was reduced by 218 miles because of 18 cutoffs (Elliott, 1932, page 59).

Title: Iowa: Land Of 1,000 Streams - Iowa Confluence Water Trails
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
I have a confession to make. I am not from Iowa. Even after 21 years in this state, it is hard to give up my identity as a Minnesotan. And despite all of the Iowa Nice, I don’t always feel like I belong here. People here have deep roots. I live in the “big city,” but it seems to me like everyone here has connections to family in small towns that branch out and twist around each other generation after generation, like a tangle of vines. Communities here feel tight, and sometimes impenetrable, but also safe.
Iowa definitely grows on you though. New memories sprout with each new person, place and experience, until all of the sudden, you realize you have become firmly planted in the prairie! My best memories and strongest connections to this state — its small towns, its quiet landscapes and its beautiful people — have been built by following Iowa’s waterways. The stories and lessons that I am hoping to share in this blog are mostly about Beaver Creek, but I hope that my stories inspire others to tell tales of their unique place of wonder.

#### Iowa Waterways
If you look at a map of Iowa, you don’t see a bunch of lakes, like you do in much of Minnesota, Land of 10,000 Lakes (technically 11,842). Instead, what stands out are the branching paths of the rivers running southwest to the Missouri River or east to the mighty Mississippi. Each of these streams is shaped by a different combination of geology, plants, animals, people and time, as they meander downhill.
![Image 1: Map of all the streams in Iowa with one highlighted in pink near the center of the state](https://www.iconwatertrails.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/streamsiniowa-e1635282798944.png)_Streams in Iowa (3rd order and above) with Beaver Creek in pink._
I wonder if anyone has ever tried to count the streams in Iowa. I make a lot of maps, so you would think that this would be an easy task for me . . . but it really isn’t. If you only look at the main stems of each river system, like the trunk of a tree with many branches, you see less than 100. But if you start with the smallest tributaries (the first order streams), there are over 300,000 in Iowa!
Another way to quantify the abundance of waterways in this state is to count by watershed. There are 56 HUC 8 watersheds that contain our big river systems. These big watersheds can be broken into 1,717 smaller watersheds, called HUC 12 watersheds. The average size of these small watersheds is 35 square miles. If you drain water off of 35 square miles and add some groundwater flow, you should have plenty of water to support a perennial (always flowing) stream. This means that most Iowans have a stream big enough to splash in only a short distance away. When Iowa isn’t in the middle of a drought (ahem, 2020!), we all have a fishable and floatable river not too far away, too!

#### Beaver Creek
It is easy to take these streams for granted. There are so many, and maybe they don’t seem as dramatic as the rushing rivers of the Grand Canyon, as spectacular as Niagara Falls or as clean as we would like them to be. But our everyday experiences are touched by these streams, and there are many wonders to be found in them if you are willing to look. My family lives in the Beaver Creek watershed in the northwest corner of Polk County. This hidden gem flows through farm fields, small towns, past a military training facility, behind the greenhouses of seed companies and though suburban neighborhoods before it joins the Des Moines River, 77 miles and three counties from where it begins. It is a great place to explore at all times of the year!
![Image 2: Black and white photo of a girl crouched down next to the water](https://www.iconwatertrails.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/girlbywater.jpeg)
My family likes to wander down to Beaver Creek in the spring to check out the woodland wildflowers and watch for migrating birds. In the summer, we go to cool off in the water, skip rocks and play in the mud and sand. When I need alone time (as all parents do!), I head to my favorite trail through the greenbelt for an hour or two. Thanks to the new access at NW 70th in Johnston, I can even fit a couple of hours of floating in after work provided there is enough flow. My favorite time of year is winter, when the little mountain bike trails are not overgrown and you can follow the banks of the stream for miles. Having access to nature close to home is what has kept me sane (mostly!) through the COVID-19 pandemic. 2020 has reminded us how important it is to have beauty and fresh air and places to get away from the noise and the news!
I still haven’t come up with a good way to count the streams in Iowa, so I am going to make up a number. I wouldn’t want to be seen as trying to outdo my friends up north! We are all humble Midwesterners after all. And regardless of the number, these streams are one of the things that makes Iowa really special. All of us have a little slice of heaven close to home in this Land of 1,000 Streams.

#### Beaver Creek
Now it’s time to get away from the screen and go explore — see you on the trails!
![Image 3: A bridge going across water and leaves on either side of the river are turning colors in fall](https://www.iconwatertrails.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/BridgeinFall.png)![Image 4: A woman in a blue shirt and a girl in a dark colored shirt taking a selfie next to the river](https://www.iconwatertrails.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Selfie.jpeg)

She is a geologist, a PhD in environmental science and has been a DNR employee for 17 years. If you see someone getting pulled down the trail by two sled dogs, it is probably her._

**Hannibal Hamlin** (August 27, 1809 – July 4, 1891) was an American politician and diplomat who was the 15th [vice president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_president_of_the_United_States "Vice president of the United States"), serving from 1861 to 1865, during President [Abraham Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln "Abraham Lincoln")'s first term. He was the first [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") vice president.

As an attorney from [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine"), Hamlin began his political career as a [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") in the Maine House of Representatives before being elected twice to the [United States House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives"), and then to the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). With his strong [abolitionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionist "Abolitionist") views, he left the Democratic Party for the newly formed Republican Party in 1856. In the [1860 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1860_United_States_presidential_election "1860 United States presidential election"), Hamlin balanced the successful Republican ticket as a New Englander partnered with the Midwesterner Lincoln. Although not a close friend of the president, he lent loyal support to his key projects such as the [Emancipation Proclamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emancipation_Proclamation "Emancipation Proclamation") during the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War").
In the [1864 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1864_United_States_presidential_election "1864 United States presidential election"), Hamlin was replaced as vice-presidential nominee by [Andrew Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Johnson "Andrew Johnson"), a [Southern Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Democrats "Southern Democrats") from [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee") who remained loyal to the union, and chosen for his appeal to [Southern Unionists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Unionists "Southern Unionists"). After being appointed Collector of the Port of Boston, Hamlin was elected to two more terms in the Senate, and finally served as [U.S. Minister to Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_Spain "List of ambassadors of the United States to Spain") before retiring in 1882.

[![Image 3](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Younger_Hannibal_Hamlin.jpg/250px-Younger_Hannibal_Hamlin.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Younger_Hannibal_Hamlin.jpg)
Hamlin c.late 1840s
Hamlin was born to Cyrus Hamlin and Anna ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name")Livermore) in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris,_Maine "Paris, Maine") (now in [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine"), then a part of [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts")). He was a sixth-generation descendant of English colonist James Hamlin, who had settled in [Barnstable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnstable,_Massachusetts "Barnstable, Massachusetts"), part of the [Plymouth Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth_Colony "Plymouth Colony") in 1639.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal_Hamlin#cite_note-1) He was a grandnephew of U.S. Senator [Samuel Livermore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Livermore "Samuel Livermore") II[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal_Hamlin#cite_note-lifeandtimes-2) of New Hampshire.
According to folklore, Hamlin's life was saved when he was an infant by a [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States")[medicine woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicine_man "Medicine man") named [Molly Ockett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly_Ockett "Molly Ockett"). Hamlin was gravely ill, and Ockett prescribed that he be given warm cow's milk, after which he recovered.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal_Hamlin#cite_note-:0-3)

Hamlin attended the district schools and [Hebron Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebron_Academy "Hebron Academy") and later managed his father's farm. From 1827 to 1830 he published the _Oxford Jeffersonian_ newspaper in partnership with [Horatio King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horatio_King "Horatio King").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal_Hamlin#cite_note-4)
He studied law with the firm headed by [Samuel Fessenden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Fessenden "Samuel Fessenden"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal_Hamlin#cite_note-5) was admitted to the bar in 1833, and began practicing in [Hampden, Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampden,_Maine "Hampden, Maine"), where he lived until 1848.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal_Hamlin#cite_note-6)
Hamlin married Sarah Jane Emery of Paris Hill in 1833. Her father was Stephen Emery, who was appointed as [Maine's Attorney General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine_Attorney_General "Maine Attorney General") from 1839 to 1840.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal_Hamlin#cite_note-7) Hamlin and Sarah had four children: George, [Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Hamlin_(general) "Charles Hamlin (general)"), [Cyrus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrus_Hamlin_(general) "Cyrus Hamlin (general)"), and Sarah.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal_Hamlin#cite_note-8)

From a small town in Maine to the brink of shaping a divided nation, Hannibal Hamlin’s remarkable—and often overlooked—journey to the vice presidency is one of America’s greatest “what ifs.”
Hannibal Hamlin was born in Paris, Maine in 1809. He ultimately became the first Mainer to ever become vice president of the United States, serving alongside Abraham Lincoln, but Hamlin’s rise to the top did not come easy.
"Hannibal Hamlin is one of the great might have-beens of Maine history and one of the great should-have-beens of American history,” Maine historian Herb Adams said.
Adams says Hamlin’s political path often goes unnoticed.
![Image 15: Hannibal Hamlin (Maine Historic Preservation Commission)](https://wgme.com/resources/media2/16x9/1280/800/center/80/5ccf23c3-9b2c-4672-b106-a161d9a1c2c1-PAA250HANNIBALHAMLIN.transfer_frame_3602.jpeg)

# From Maine to the White House: Hannibal Hamlin's unlikely rise
#### topics:
"He was one of the most successful politicians in Maine history but least remembered for it,” Adams said.
Hamlin became the youngest speaker of the Maine House of Representatives and was so committed to ending slavery, he even switched political parties.
"Because of the Democratic Party’s position on slavery that is defending it in the South and not believing in the equality of Blacks. On the floor of the Senate, he said, ‘I love my country more than I love my party.’ And became a member of the brand-new political party the Republicans,” Adams said.
By 1860 the Lincoln-Hamlin ticket was formed and in 1861
"They won with about 39 percent of the vote, not getting a single vote in the South,” Adams said.
The country remained divided and the relationship between Lincoln and Hamlin was cordial at best.
"They were associates. They were never friends. They never became friends. They were two horses attached to the same wagon but not attached to each other,” Adams said.
While still serving as vice president, Hamlin decided to come back home.
![Image 16: Hannibal Hamlin (Maine Historic Preservation Commission)](https://wgme.com/resources/media2/16x9/1280/800/center/80/57260f97-8e79-4c56-b7a3-ae5913828612-PAA250HANNIBALHAMLIN.transfer_frame_3087.jpeg)

"Hamlin went and joined the Coast Guard in Maine and served a stint during the Civil War as a soldier peeling potatoes and standing guard in Kittery,” Adams said.
Hamlin was bumped off the ticket in March of 1865, one month later Lincoln was tragically assassinated.

“One of the great what ifs of American history, deserves to be remembered for the good man he was and for that which maybe he could have done for his country,” Adams said.
During his later years it was Hamlin who suggested that Abraham Lincoln’s birthday become a national holiday. Hamlin died on July 4, 1891 while playing cards at the Tarratine Club in Bangor.

**Hannibal Hamlin** (August 27, 1809 – July 4, 1891) was an American politician and diplomat who was the 15th [vice president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_president_of_the_United_States "Vice president of the United States"), serving from 1861 to 1865, during President [Abraham Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln "Abraham Lincoln")'s first term. As an attorney from [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine"), Hamlin began his political career as a [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") in the Maine House of Representatives before being elected twice to the [United States House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives"), and then to the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). With his strong [abolitionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionist "Abolitionist") views, he left the Democratic Party for the newly formed Republican Party in 1856. Although not a close friend of the president, he lent loyal support to his key projects such as the [Emancipation Proclamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emancipation_Proclamation "Emancipation Proclamation") during the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War").
In the [1864 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1864_United_States_presidential_election "1864 United States presidential election"), Hamlin was replaced as vice-presidential nominee by [Andrew Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Johnson "Andrew Johnson"), a [Southern Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Democrats "Southern Democrats") from [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee") who remained loyal to the union, and chosen for his appeal to [Southern Unionists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Unionists "Southern Unionists"). After being appointed Collector of the Port of Boston, Hamlin was elected to two more terms in the Senate, and finally served as [U.S. Minister to Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_Spain "List of ambassadors of the United States to Spain") before retiring in 1882.

The **Council of Three Fires**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Three_Fires#cite_note-1) is a long-standing alliance of the [Ojibwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe "Ojibwe"), [Odawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa "Odawa"), and [Potawatomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potawatomi "Potawatomi"), three [Anishinaabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anishinaabe "Anishinaabe") peoples who are [Indigenous peoples of the Northeastern Woodlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Northeastern_Woodlands "Indigenous peoples of the Northeastern Woodlands").

Originally one people or a collection of closely related bands, the distinct identities of [Ojibwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe "Ojibwe"), [Odawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odawa "Odawa"), and [Potawatomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potawatomi "Potawatomi") developed after the Anishinaabe reached [Michilimackinac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michilimackinac "Michilimackinac") on their [journey westward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_fires_prophecy "Seven fires prophecy") from the Atlantic coast.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Three_Fires#cite_note-2) Using the [Midewiwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midewiwin "Midewiwin")[scrolls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birch_bark_scrolls "Birch bark scrolls"), Potawatomi elder Shup-Shewana dated the formation of the Council of Three Fires to 796 AD at Michilimackinac.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Three_Fires#cite_note-3) In this council, the Ojibwe were addressed as the "Older Brother", the Odawa as the "Middle Brother", and the Potawatomi as the "Younger Brother".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Three_Fires#cite_note-4) Consequently, whenever the three Anishinaabe nations are mentioned in this specific _and_ consecutive order of Ojibwe, Odawa, and Potawatomi, it is an indicator implying Council of Three Fires as well.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

**Hannibal Hamlin Garland** (September 14, 1860 – March 4, 1940) was an American novelist, poet, essayist, short story writer, [Georgist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgist "Georgist"), and [psychical researcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parapsychology "Parapsychology"). He is best known for his fiction involving hard-working [Midwestern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Midwest "American Midwest") farmers.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamlin_Garland#cite_note-1)
Hannibal Hamlin Garland was born on a farm near [West Salem, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Salem,_Wisconsin "West Salem, Wisconsin"), on September 14, 1860, the second of four children of Richard Garland of [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine") and Charlotte Isabelle McClintock.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamlin_Garland#cite_note-2) The boy was named after [Hannibal Hamlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal_Hamlin "Hannibal Hamlin"), the vice-president under [Abraham Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln "Abraham Lincoln").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamlin_Garland#cite_note-3) He lived on various Midwestern farms throughout his young life, but settled in [Boston, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston,_Massachusetts "Boston, Massachusetts"), in 1884 to pursue a career in writing.

He read diligently in the [Boston Public Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Public_Library "Boston Public Library").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamlin_Garland#cite_note-eb-4) There he became enamored with the ideas of [Henry George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_George "Henry George"), and his Single Tax Movement.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamlin_Garland#cite_note-Garland1998-5) George's ideas came to influence a number of his works, such as _[Main-Travelled Roads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main-Travelled\_Roads "Main-Travelled Roads")_ (1891), _Prairie Folks_ (1892), and his novel _[Jason Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason\_Edwards:\_An\_Average\_Man "Jason Edwards: An Average Man")_ (1892).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamlin_Garland#cite_note-6)
_Main-Travelled Roads_ was his first major success. It was a collection of short stories inspired by his days on the farm. He serialized a biography of [Ulysses S. Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant "Ulysses S. Grant") in _[McClure's Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McClure's\_Magazine "McClure's Magazine")_ before publishing it as a book in 1898. The same year, Garland traveled to the [Yukon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yukon "Yukon") to witness the [Klondike Gold Rush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klondike_Gold_Rush "Klondike Gold Rush"), which inspired _The Trail of the Gold Seekers_ (1899). He lived on a farm between [Osage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osage,_Iowa "Osage, Iowa"), and [St. Ansgar, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Ansgar,_Iowa "St. Ansgar, Iowa") for quite some time. Many of his writings are based on this era of his life.

In 1893,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamlin_Garland#cite_note-7) Hamlin moved to Chicago, where he lived at 6427 South Greenwood Avenue in the [Woodlawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodlawn,_Chicago "Woodlawn, Chicago") neighborhood. He is considered "a significant figure in the Chicago Literary Movement" and "one of Chicago's most important authors".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamlin_Garland#cite_note-MoccasinRanchPark-8) Moccasin Ranch Park, located near address, is named in his honor.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamlin_Garland#cite_note-MoccasinRanchPark-8)
In Illinois, Garland married [Zulime Taft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zulime_Taft?action=edit&redlink=1 "Zulime Taft (page does not exist)"), the sister of sculptor [Lorado Taft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorado_Taft "Lorado Taft"), and began working as a teacher and a lecturer.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamlin_Garland#cite_note-9)
A prolific writer, Garland continued to publish novels, short fiction, and essays. In 1917, he published his autobiography, _A Son of the Middle Border_. The book's success prompted a sequel, _A Daughter of the Middle Border_, for which Garland won the 1922 [Pulitzer Prize for Biography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_Biography "Pulitzer Prize for Biography"). After two more volumes, Garland began a second series of memoirs based on his diary. Garland became quite well known during his lifetime and had many friends in literary circles.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamlin_Garland#cite_note-10) He was made a member of the [American Academy of Arts and Letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Academy_of_Arts_and_Letters "American Academy of Arts and Letters") in 1918.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamlin_Garland#cite_note-eb-4)

Garland became quite well known during his lifetime and had many friends in literary circles.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamlin_Garland#cite_note-10) He was made a member of the [American Academy of Arts and Letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Academy_of_Arts_and_Letters "American Academy of Arts and Letters") in 1918.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamlin_Garland#cite_note-eb-4)
